description: One of the smallest flowering plants: a free-floating green oval frond 2-4 mm across with a single root hanging beneath, budding off new fronds so fast that it covers a still pond in a bright green skin in summer. It grows on the still water of ponds, sloughs and quiet backwaters, drifting with the wind into the corners.

season_notes.winter: A thin, scattered film; many fronds sink to the bottom as resting buds until spring.
season_notes.spring: Fronds rise and multiply as the water warms, spreading from the pond edges.
season_notes.summer: A continuous bright green carpet on still water, broken by every animal that wades through.
season_notes.fall: Still green, thinning as the water cools.

riparian.water: Floats on still, sheltered, fresh water that lasts through the summer, richest where the water is warm and fertile; current or wind-swept open water clears it.

notes: Common duckweed is a tiny floating aquatic of still fresh water nearly worldwide, native to California; on foothill stock ponds and mill ponds it forms a green skin in summer. Each plant is a flat, oval, slightly thick frond (a stem and leaf in one) 1-4 mm across with a single hanging root; it buds new fronds from pockets at the base, so colonies are clonal and double in a few days in warm water. Flowers are microscopic and rare (no flower block). Habit floating (new): a flat mat on the water surface, which the module draws only from above on a pond's open water; leaf shape round, 3 mm, a bright yellow-green. height_m is the frond's thickness and the hanging root, not a height that matters for drawing; height_by_month is read here as the mat's cover through the year (0.4 in winter when many fronds sink as starchy resting buds, 1.0 in summer). Zone pond_water only; orders and permanence say only that the water must be still and last the summer (orders [1, 7] is a placeholder: a pond is not a stream order). Ducks, geese and many other water birds eat it, and none is in the game's animal library yet, so eaten_by is empty. shades_water 0, though a full mat shades the water under it.
